prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated in parallel, and for its development to 10^-18 fractional uncertainty, opening new regimes of precision measurement

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B012 with Katori and Ye. The deciding argument is the one the chair asks for, namely what is new relative to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles, and Wineland's work gave control of single trapped quantum systems. Neither gave a way to interrogate a large ensemble of neutral atoms with the motional (Doppler and recoil) shifts removed and the dominant trapping light shift cancelled at the same time. The magic-wavelength lattice does exactly that. It is a distinct concept (Katori's proposal and first demonstration) that changes the statistics: thousands of atoms give a stability that a single ion cannot reach in a reasonable averaging time, which is what made systematic uncertainty evaluation at 10^-18 practical. Ye's group then took it to the accuracy frontier and showed that spin-exchange and density effects in a degenerate lattice gas could be controlled and even used. The 10^-18 level has been reached and cross-checked by several independent laboratories, so this is a verified experimental result and not a roadmap. It already supports millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements, clock-comparison limits on drifting constants and ultralight dark matter, and the case for redefining the second. I do not think a realised fundamental-physics discovery or the redefinition itself is a precondition; the demonstrated measurement capability is what the prize should recognise, in the way the committee has honoured other instruments whose major discoveries came afterwards.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses remain. First, a skeptical reader can call this a maturing refinement of a program already honoured twice, and trapped-ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) reached comparable uncertainty by another route, so the citation has to be narrow about the lattice architecture. Second, credit beyond two names is open: Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Bloom, Hinkley and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE teams made substantial contributions, and none of us has a verified priority record. I would want an expert report from the clock community before the final vote, and the committee should accept that three-person limits make some omissions unavoidable. Third, the fundamental-physics reach is so far limits, not a detection, and relativistic geodesy and the redefinition of the second are still prospective. I would therefore anchor the citation on the demonstrated 10^-18 performance rather than on those applications.

responses.point: Johansson asked me to say how I would answer the objection that the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion prize already cover this territory, and noted that Ye's group made spin-exchange and density effects a controlled part of the clock.
responses.response: My answer is that the two earlier prizes supplied a ruler and a controlled single quantum system, while the lattice clock supplies a third thing: a large ensemble of neutral atoms with first-order Doppler, recoil and trap light shifts simultaneously removed. That is what changed the averaging statistics and made 10^-18 evaluation feasible in hours rather than weeks, and it is why a single-ion clock is not the same achievement. I accept your physics point and would put it in the argument for the prize: the many-body regime is part of why this is more than a better number. It also means the citation should name the lattice and the many-atom regime explicitly. I do not think the committee needs the redefinition of the second to have happened first.

responses.point: Olsson regards B012 as the safest consensus option but not the strongest invention, and says B032 (aberration-corrected electron optics with Rose, Haider and Krivanek) has more discovery content, while acknowledging that Knut Urban is omitted.
responses.response: I respect the invention case for B032, and as an experimentalist I value a corrector that was built, reproduced and commercialised. Two things keep me from moving. The Urban omission and the unverified TEM versus STEM priority split mean we cannot defend a three-name credit today, and you have said so yourself. Second, the physics prize has usually recognised instruments whose own capability opened new measurements in physics; the lattice clock does that directly through gravitational redshift, constants and dark-matter searches, while the main impact of aberration correction is in materials and chemistry. I do not think B012 wins only because it offends nobody: it wins because its attribution is clear and its measurement is reproduced independently. If you still prefer B032, I would like the committee to hear what a microscopy expert says about priority before the vote.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B018 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp), calls the clock case his strongest challenge, defers to Lindroth and me on the physics, and says he would accept B012 if topological matter fails to reach agreement.
responses.response: I appreciate that, and I agree that B018 is mature and that the 2016 prize leaves room for the Z2 classification. My difficulty is with credit, not merit: the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal of HgTe and the 3D Fu-Kane-Mele strand cannot be handled inside three names, and Zhang's death makes a clean repair impossible. I therefore keep B018 as my first alternative, and I would not describe a clock prize as a defeat for topological matter; a later cycle with a better-defined credit is plausible. On your question of what is new in the clock beyond an improved number, I have tried to answer it in my reply to Johansson. I would ask only that if the committee goes to B012, you and others who are outside this area hold me to the standard of an explicit, narrow citation.

responses.point: Pearce, who prefers B012 after opening with IceCube first, warns that relativistic geodesy and the redefinition of the second are still prospective, and suggests anchoring the citation on demonstrated 10^-18 performance and the new fundamental-physics reach.
responses.response: I accept that correction and have changed my citation accordingly: it now names the invention of the lattice clock and the demonstrated 10^-18 uncertainty, and speaks of new regimes of precision measurement without promising geodesy or a redefinition. I also take your point that consensus is not scientific merit, which is why I have argued for B012 on what a single trapped-ion clock cannot do. On IceCube, I agree with the chair that it is a strong candidate in the next few cycles, but with TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane as the main source associations and DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA predecessors, I still judge it maturing rather than mature for a two-name credit this year.

responses.point: Lindroth wants the citation to stress the lattice scheme, the many-atom regime and what the precision lets us measure, rather than precision as such, and is uncertain whether single-ion optical clocks belong in the citation.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and have rewritten the citation around the magic-wavelength lattice and parallel interrogation. I would keep single-ion clocks out of the citation: they are a parallel route recognised in part in 2012, and including them would either expand the credited names beyond the limit or dilute the distinctness argument. As a check on priority, your theory perspective on the magic-wavelength condition and my own uncertainty about Lemonde and Takamoto are exactly why I would ask for an external clock-community report before the final vote.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is a distinct achievement from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I think the argument is strong but others have not conceded it.

Whether Katori and Ye are the right two names given Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Bloom, Hinkley and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE contributions; an external expert report would help and I cannot verify priority from the supplied record.
Whether timing relative to the redefinition of the second matters; I lean to treating demonstrated 10^-18 performance as sufficient.

Whether a second part from another field (for example B018 or B022 once the attribution or maturity issues are resolved) would make a stronger prize than the single achievement, given the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD, which is adjacent to the JILA lineage of Ye, and Lund atomic physics sits in the same broad precision-spectroscopy community. I have no direct collaboration with Katori or Ye and see no recusal need; the chair has noted this and the committee may weigh it as it sees fit.
